candidates.attacker_control: The attacker supplies the HTML string passed to AntiSamy.scan()/scan(html, policy, AntiSamy.SAX). Element name and attributes are fully attacker-controlled. A request-side payload such as <style onload="...">p{color:red}</style> is parsed by NekoHTML, and because the style tag is in the policy with action=validate, the element is kept and written back with the attacker's attributes verbatim. Content must yield non-empty cleaned CSS, otherwise the element is dropped (MagicSAXFilter.java:170-172).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the DOM implementation (AntiSamyDOMScanner.actionValidate + processAttributes) which does validate the style element's attributes and drops unlisted ones, so the behavior is path-specific, not an unavoidable parser limitation. Checked that the CSS TEXT itself is scanned (scanStyleSheet) and that cleaned CSS values are constrained by policy css-rules, so this is not merely 'CSS injection'; the defect is in the attribute channel. Checked that the style element is only emitted when cleaned CSS is non-empty, and that the attribute loop at lines 283-351 is bypassed specifically by the CSS branch. Checked whether the policy already forbids such attributes: it does (antisamy.xml style rule lists type/media only), so passing them through is contrary to the loaded policy. No test or runtime evidence exists in this snapshot to demonstrate browser execution of the surviving handler, so the XSS impact is a lead, not a confirmed exploit. Also considered that upstream AntiSamy may retain this structure, which lowers confidence that this exact spot is the fixed CVE, but does not remove the source-level validation gap.
candidates.impact: Whitelist/policy bypass in the sanitizer's default path: attributes that the policy explicitly does not allow on <style> (notably event handlers and unknown attributes) are preserved in the sanitized output. Where the browser executes the surviving handler, this yields script execution in the context of pages rendering AntiSamy-cleaned HTML (XSS); at minimum it defeats the attribute whitelist for the style element and allows CSS/markup-affecting attributes through although the DOM path drops them. Because the output is then consumed by the victim browser, the security impact is carried across the trust boundary.
candidates.prerequisites: Application calls the default SAX scan path (AntiSamy.scan(String) uses scanType=SAX; AntiSamy.java:78, AntiSamy.java:96-103). Active policy must define a <style> tag with action=validate (true for all bundled policies, e.g. antisamy.xml:806). For script execution the browser must honor the surviving handler on a style element (e.g. onload on <style>/<link>), which is the intended XSS impact and was not runtime-verified here.
candidates.root_cause: In MagicSAXFilter.startElement, when a tag has action 'validate' and is the style element, the filter takes the CSS branch and stores the raw incoming XMLAttributes in `cssAttributes` (MagicSAXFilter.java:272-277). The per-attribute validation loop (lines 283-351) is only executed in the non-style branch, so the style element's attributes are never checked against the policy. At endElement for Ops.CSS the filter writes the element back with those raw attributes: `super.startElement(element, cssAttributes, new AugmentationsImpl())` (MagicSAXFilter.java:178-182), i.e., every attribute and value the attacker supplied on <style> (onload/onerror handlers, invalid type/media values, unknown attributes) survives into the sanitized output. The DOM scanner does not behave this way: AntiSamyDOMScanner.actionValidate sends the style element through processAttributes (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:359-371), so unsupported attributes such as onload are removed there (default antisamy.xml style rule allows only type/media, lines 806-813), demonstrating the intended policy behavior.
candidates.title: SAX scan path re-emits the <style> element's original, unvalidated attributes (policy/whitelist bypass on the default scan path)
candidates.trace: AntiSamy.scan(taintedHTML) -> AntiSamy.scan(..., SAX) -> AntiSamySAXScanner.scan -> NekoHTML SAXParser -> MagicSAXFilter.startElement: tag=style, action=validate, isStyle -> operations.push(CSS); cssContent=new StringBuffer(); cssAttributes=attributes (raw, unfiltered). characters() accumulates CSS. endElement: Ops.CSS -> cssScanner.scanStyleSheet(...) -> if cleaned CSS non-empty: super.startElement(element, cssAttributes, ...) emits the original attributes; super.characters(cleaned CSS); super.endElement(...). Output serializer (ASHTMLSerializer/ASXHTMLSerializer) writes those attributes into the returned clean HTML.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and the project's tests are absent from the snapshot, so I could not confirm (a) that NekoHTML preserves/forwards the handler attribute exactly as read, (b) that the chosen browser fires onload/onerror for an inline <style> element, or (c) that no later output filter removes the attribute. Dependencies (nekohtml 1.9.22, batik-css 1.8, commons-httpclient 3.1) are declared in pom.xml but their actual jars/behaviors were not inspectable in this run.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper input validation / attribute whitelist bypass in HTML sanitizer (CWE-79/CWE-20 class)

coverage_summary: All 48 files visible to the tooling were enumerated. I read in full or near-full the scan pipeline sources (AntiSamy, AbstractAntiSamyScanner, AntiSamyDOMScanner, AntiSamySAXScanner, MagicSAXFilter, ASHTMLSerializer, ASXHTMLSerializer, Constants, Policy, InternalPolicy, CleanResults, Tag, Attribute, Property, AntiSamyPattern, TagMatcher, CssScanner, CssHandler, CssValidator, ExternalCssScanner, URIUtils, XMLUtil, HTMLEntityEncoder, ErrorMessageUtil) and skimmed the policy XMLs via full reads of their directives, common-regexps, common-attributes, global-tag-attributes, style/img/embed/object/link rules, allowed-empty-tags and targeted greps of tag/css rules for event handlers, javascript:, srcdoc and javascript literals. No test sources are present in the snapshot. Static read only; nothing was compiled, executed, or fuzzed, and dependency jars were not available for inspection. AntiSamy.scan(String) uses the SAX path by default, so SAX-side findings are prioritized.
limitations: No execution, compilation, tests, or dependency-jar inspection was possible, so parser/serializer behavior (NekoHTML attribute handling, Xalan/Xerces attribute escaping, browser style-element load events) is reasoned from source only and not runtime-confirmed.

The snapshot contains no test code and no VCS history, so intended-vs-regressed behavior could not be diffed against upstream; statements about 'intended' behavior rely on comparing the DOM and SAX code paths and the bundled policy.

The policy XML files (up to ~80 KB each) were reviewed selectively (directives, common attributes, global attributes, tag rules for style/img/embed/object/link/script, allowed-empty-tags, and greps of css-rules), not line-by-line in full; a weakened policy regex elsewhere cannot be fully excluded.

The candidate is a lead with medium confidence: the attribute-passthrough is clearly present in source and contradicts the loaded policy, but the XSS impact step (browser executing a surviving handler attribute on <style>) was not verified and some upstream versions appear to share this code shape.
A rejected lead (removePI NullPointerException) could not have its reachability confirmed because the NekoHTML parser is not available in the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: AntiSamyDOMScanner.removePI() detaches the node and then calls node.getParentNode().removeChild(node) on the now-detached node (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:686-690) -> guaranteed NullPointerException if a ProcessingInstruction node is ever produced; uncaught by scan() (only SAXException/IOException are handled), i.e. attacker-triggerable denial of service.
rejected_leads.reason: Real code defect but impact is availability only, and reachability depends on NekoHTML DOMFragmentParser emitting ProcessingInstruction nodes for untrusted HTML, which I could not verify without the parser sources/jars; also less aligned with a sanitizer security fix than the attribute-passthrough candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter treats any attribute named style as valid regardless of whether the tag/policy allows it (MagicSAXFilter.java:293-304 runs before the attribute==null branch); the DOM scanner requires attr!=null (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:533).
rejected_leads.reason: In the bundled policy style is a global-tag-attribute (antisamy.xml:494-497), so the bypass has no effect by default; the CSS value is still policy-filtered. Policy-dependent, low demonstrated impact.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter computes isStyle with the reversed expression "style".endsWith(element.localpart) (MagicSAXFilter.java:272) instead of equality.
rejected_leads.reason: Only true for localparts that are suffixes of 'style' (style/styl/.../e). No such tag exists in the bundled policies, so it is effectively equivalent to equals for default configurations; no exploitation path found.

rejected_leads.lead: AntiSamyDOMScanner.stripNonValidXMLCharacters only removes invalid XML characters when the whole input matches the invalid-character class (uses Matcher.matches() instead of find(), AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:786-793), so stripping is effectively never performed despite the comment that it prevents NekoHTML from breaking on hostile encodings.
rejected_leads.reason: Sanitization control is ineffective rather than a demonstrable injection primitive; the SAX path never strips at all and I found no source evidence of an exploitable parser-differential in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: ExternalCssScanner performs server-side HTTP GETs for @import URLs supplied in untrusted CSS when the policy enables embedStyleSheets (ExternalCssScanner.java:73-173; CssHandler.java:214-281), with host/port unrestricted (only scheme/format regexes checked). Potential SSRF.
rejected_leads.reason: Disabled in every bundled policy (embedStyleSheets=false), explicitly documented as opt-in functionality, and requires a non-default policy; not the strongest source-evidenced issue.

rejected_leads.lead: SAX path emits <param> masquerading output using the original name/value and does not copy the DOM conversion semantics; and the parameter-based embed path passes attacker-created attribute names in the DOM path (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:341-351).
rejected_leads.reason: Traced the flows: created attributes are still run through the attribute whitelist and invalid names cause DOMException (DoS, not injection); no XSS path established for default policies.

summary: Coverage: the snapshot is OWASP AntiSamy 1.5.5-SNAPSHOT (Java HTML sanitizer, 48 visible files: 26 Java sources, 11 policy XMLs, 11 resource bundles, pom/README). I read every Java source that participates in the scan pipeline (AntiSamy, Policy/InternalPolicy, AntiSamyDOMScanner, AntiSamySAXScanner, MagicSAXFilter, serializers, Attribute/Tag/Property, CssScanner/CssHandler/CssValidator/ExternalCssScanner, URIUtils, HTMLEntityEncoder, XMLUtil, ErrorMessageUtil, CleanResults, TagMatcher) and grepped the policy resources for dangerous attributes/regexes. `AntiSamy.scan(String)` defaults to the SAX path (scanType = SAX), so `MagicSAXFilter` is the primary trust-boundary code. The single strongest source-evidenced issue I found is that in the default SAX path the `<style>` element's original, unvalidated attributes are retained and re-emitted into the sanitized output. I could not run anything, so all statements are static-read only.
